Excellencies, distinguished representatives, dear colleagues, I hereby declare open the 63rd regular session of the Human Rights Council. It is my honor to welcome Mr. Walker Turk, the High Commissioner for Human Rights. It is also a special pleasure to welcome six delegates who are here thanks to the generous support of the donors to the Voluntary Technical Assistance Trust Fund to support the participation of least developed countries and small island developing states in the work of the Council. The delegates are from Angola, Barbados, Benin, Cambodia, Jamaica and the Marshall Islands. We look forward to their active participation in the Council. Distinguished representatives, allow me to address a few organizational and procedural matters. During the organizational meeting on 24th of August, we discussed the draft program of work for the 63rd session. Following the Council's adoption of extraordinary cost and time saving measures on that day, the session is expected to close on Wednesday, 7 October, and the latest draft of the program of work dated 25th August. Reflecting this adjustment is available on the Council's portal. Let me thank you in advance for your cooperation in respecting the speaking time limit in order to complete our work on time. At this point, are there any delegations wishing to take the floor to make comments on the draft programme of work as it currently stands? I see no request for the floor. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, I now propose that the Council approve the draft program of work with the understanding that it is a living document. I encourage everyone to regularly check the SCAD website or applications for the latest updates. Does any member of the Council wish to comment on this proposal? I see none. If I see no objection, the program of work of our this session is approved. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, the events online system for inscription on the list of speakers for all general debates, interactive dialogues and panel discussions opened on Monday, 31 August at 10 a.m. and will close two hours before the meeting in which the respective dialogue or discussion is scheduled to begin. Once the online inscription has closed, delegations may still inscribe or withdraw by sending an e-mail to the list of speakers desk. The list of speakers will close approximately 15 minutes after the beginning of each debate. The procedure for the registration for the list of speakers for panel discussions and interactive dialogues will be the same as previous sessions. Interested states will be asked to rank panels and interactive dialogues in the order of their priorities. Speaking slots will be allocated by the system taking into account their priorities. If the number of states indicating the highest priority for a particular debate exceeds the maximum number of available speaking slots, the slots will be allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. The online system for inscription on the list of speakers for the adoptions of UPR will open on Monday, 14 September at 9am and close on Thursday, 17 September at 6pm. No inscriptions will be possible after this deadline. For National Human Rights Institutions and non-governmental organizations, the list of speakers for all debates during the session opened online on Tuesday, 00 p.m. For indigenous peoples, the list of speakers for the interactive dialogues with Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and with the Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, as well as for the annual panel discussions on the rights of indigenous peoples, also open online on 1st September at 2:00 PM via the events platform. In order to balance the importance of inclusivity and what is feasible in terms of time and resources, the list of speakers for NGOs for each of the general debates will be set in line with the average number of NGOs that participated in each of the general debates in the previous three September sessions. So that is the 60th, 57th, and 54th sessions. I kindly request that all participants upload the Word version of their oral statements through the online system for the list of speakers. If this is not possible, please send them by e-mail to conference services and the Council Secretariat. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, Allow me to recall that the deadline for the submission of draft proposals for the 63rd session is Thursday, 24 September at 1:00 p.m. Geneva time. I encourage sponsors to table proposals as early as possible. The submission of a proposal after the deadline needs the prior approval by the Council before it is registered by the Secretariat. Only under exceptional circumstances would an extension of the deadline for the submission of draft proposals be approved by the Council, and for a maximum of 24 hours. Let me also underline that in accordance with resolution 5/1, delegations are invited to conduct open-ended informal consultations to secure broadest possible support for their initiatives. At least one open-ended informal consultation should be held on each draft resolutions and/or decisions before it is considered for action by the Council. I encourage delegation to continue strengthening coordination and dialogue among main sponsors, including those focusing on similar issues, and to consult with the co-facilitators for rationalization and efficiency with a view to advance the Council's endeavor to advance rationalization and efficiency. In the interest of ensuring the effective participation of all stakeholders in the work of the Human Rights Council, I encourage main sponsors of draft proposals to share draft texts with civil society organizations and other observers that follow informal consultations. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, the effective conduct of the Council sessions as well as the fulfilment of its mandate rests upon a constructive, safe and respectful environment, as all of you are aware of. Disagreement with mandate holders and their reports can always be expressed. However, it should be unacceptable to all of us and it should be unacceptable for them to be insulted, personally attacked, threatened or subjected to efforts aimed at undermining their independence and integrity when discharging their mandates. Let me also reiterate my deep concern and regret, as I'm sure it's shared by most, if not all of you, at the personal attacks and unlawful actions directed against certain mandate holders of the Council. Such practices are incompatible with the spirit of cooperation and dialogue that must underpin our work. As President, I will support them in the face of any inappropriate attacks. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, Let me emphasize that it is in our common interest to have an environment of trust and safety at the Council. States should prevent and ensure adequate protection against any act of intimidation or reprisals against individuals and groups who cooperate or have cooperated with the United Nations, its representatives and mechanisms in the field of human rights, as affirmed in Council resolution 16/21. Intimidation and reprisals can take many forms. They may occur against those who engage during council sessions, in or outside the assembly hall, or at other council-related meetings, UPR working group sessions, or during the national process, with special procedures during their visits or when sending information to mandate holders. Experts and panelists invited to participate in the Council meetings may also be affected. It is our obligation to ensure that intimidation or reprisals for cooperation with the United Nations in human rights will not happen under any circumstances. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, turning to zero tolerance towards harassment, Let me also emphasize that the United Nations, including this Council, has a zero tolerance for any form of harassment, including sexual harassment. The UNOCHP Director-General has pledged to implement the Code of Conduct to prevent harassment, including sexual harassment, at UN system events. The Bureau encourages all participants, including States and NGOs, and to be aware of and fully uphold the zero tolerance policy and comply with the code of conduct. Delegations chairing informal consultations should consider reminding participants in the meeting of the rules of participation to help prevent such incidents. So this is a responsibility broadly shared among all of us that would be also chairing meetings. On a related matter, allow me to thank the UN Security and Safety Service of the United Nations Office in Geneva for its continuous support for the Council. The Service has confirmed a continuous security presence in the Assembly Hall throughout the session. I appreciate its commitment to the safe and secure conduct of our work, particularly given the operational constraint it currently faces. Moreover, allow me to recall that Her Excellency, Ambassador Caroline Ziade, Permanent Representative of Lebanon, is serving this Council as gender focal point, including for cases of sexual harassment at meetings and events of the Human Rights Council. encourage everyone to refer to the webpage on the conduct of participants in the meetings and events of the Human Rights Council to learn more about preventing harassment and sexual harassment and how to report an incident when one does occur. All right. All complaints will be dealt with promptly. It has to be. Let me now turn to accessibility in the Council. In accordance with its resolution 16/21, the Council's Task Force on Accessibility works on improving access and participation of persons with disabilities in the work of the Council. His Excellency Ambassador Segap Kebebe Daka. is serving as chair of the task force on accessibility, and there is also a focal point for accessibility within the secretariat. Inclusion and participation of all should be the guiding principle of our work. With this, I encourage delegations to consider requesting the accessibility of mandated panel discussions to ensure live captioning and sign language interpretation. In addition, delegations are requested to upload their oral statements in Word accessibility format so they can be accessible to persons with disabilities. Captioning of video statements is also greatly encouraged. So that ends the points I need to convey on organizational matters. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, I now declare open agenda item 2, entitled Annual Report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and Reports of the Office of the High Commissioner and the Secretary-General. This agenda item will remain open throughout the session. The Human Rights Council will now hear an oral update by the High Commissioner, and I now have the pleasure of giving the floor to Mr. Volker Turk, the High Commissioner for Human Rights, for presentation. You have the floor, sir.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished participants. We live in an age of extremes. Raging wars, painful polarization, climate chaos, and head-spinning technological change make people feel disoriented and even powerless. Strong forces are working to create and sustain that feeling. Tech moguls, populists, and vested interests amplified by social media echo chambers tell us these trends are inevitable. In fact, the opposite is true. History is full of brave people who took action to resist oppression and demand their rights. People who called out injustice and inequality, people who refused to accept their fate, coming together to channel the universal values that underpin our humanity. This truth is a force to be reckoned with, underpinning all that we are doing. The past years have been marked by a growing number of armed conflicts. and diminishing respect for international human rights and humanitarian law and the United Nations Charter itself. There are now more than 60 wars involving at least one state, the highest number since the end of the Second World War. The surge in conflict between states takes us into particularly dangerous territory. I am alarmed by the resumption of attacks between the United States and Iran, affecting the entire Gulf region. Recent reports of civilian deaths and injuries, including at a wedding in Hormozgan province, are particularly concerning. The geopolitical and economic impacts of this entirely avoidable crisis are again reverberating around the world, and I appeal for an immediate return to negotiations. Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, is on a menacing trajectory, with soaring civilian casualties and intensified attacks on energy infrastructure. While the overwhelming majority of civilians killed are Ukrainians, there are also reports of growing numbers of deaths and injuries in Russia. I am horrified by reports that fully autonomous drones launched by the Russian Federation killed three Ukrainians last month. Ukraine has reportedly also field-tested such weapons, and I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement. There is only one way out of this madness: peace negotiations that respect the UN Charter. In its fourth year, the war in Sudan is expanding. Parties to the conflict continue to launch attacks on markets, hospitals, fuel stations, and other civilian infrastructure. I urge the Council to focus on the deteriorating situation in Kordofan, Blue Nile, and North and West Darfur, where civilians are at imminent risk. Again, there needs to be an immediate ceasefire, an end to foreign involvement, and a return to inclusive civilian rule. In Gaza, Israel has killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in daily strikes, despite the ceasefire that was announced almost a year ago, according to the figures from the Palestinian Ministry of Health. It continues to restrict the entry of humanitarian aid, and I am appalled by Israeli proposals for the forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and the constant stream of dehumanizing rhetoric by some senior officials. I'm also troubled that armed groups affiliated with Hamas have executed and tortured several Palestinians suspected of collaboration. In the West Bank, Israel's annexation is unfolding unobstructed despite the clear ruling of the International Court of Justice What more will it take for states to take action to prevent the entrenchment of occupation across land earmarked for Palestinians under the two-state solution? They need to end the transfer to Israel of arms that risk being used to violate international law. Companies also need to end business practices that support illegal settlements. We need far greater efforts by the international community towards sustainable peace in which Palestine and Israel live side by side in equal dignity and rights, in line with UN resolutions and international law. Words of condemnation ring hollow in the face of deliberate violations and suffering. In Lebanon, Israeli forces must end attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure. My office's assessment team is investigating violations committed by both Israel and Hezbollah since the 2nd of March, and this is crucial for truth-telling and accountability. Beyond these conflicts, there are many places around the world where people are neither at war nor at peace. Negotiations are breaking down, ceasefires are disregarded. I am concerned about renewed hostilities in South Sudan and escalating tensions in Yemen, and I urge the parties to exercise restraint and the international community to do all it can to avert a return to all-out war. And I again urge the Houthis to release at once our 73 UN and NGO colleagues who have dedicated their lives to easing the suffering of the Yemeni people. In Ethiopia, civilians are bearing the brunt of attacks in Amhara and Oromia, and of renewed tensions in Tigray. I urge all parties to end attacks against civilians and to respect international law, and I call on the government to deliver transitional justice and accountability. We will provide detailed updates on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Myanmar, and other countries later during this session. Mr. President, war reflects the failure of our humanity. The pursuit of peace embodies humanity at its best. My office will continue its vital work to prevent conflict, monitoring and documenting human rights violations, and supporting states through technical cooperation and capacity building. We will denounce all attempts to disregard international human rights and humanitarian law. And we will continue seeking ways to break cycles of violence. And I see seven entry points that I hope to pursue in the coming years. First, we will step up our analysis and advocacy around the colossal business and economic interests that fuel wars. We will not shy away from exposing the shadow players and calling for accountability. Second, we will support states to advance comprehensive transitional justice, looking at all perpetrators and centered on victims. Without truth-telling, reconciliation, and accountability, trauma and grievances turn towards vengeance and renewed violence. Third, We will continue to support mediation, including through confidence-building measures grounded in human rights. Fourth, we will work to increase women's participation and leadership in peace processes. Despite the historic role that women played as peacemakers in Ireland, in Liberia, in the Philippines, and beyond, women are largely absent from negotiations on the DRC, Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine. Fifth, We will work with grassroots organizations mobilizing for peace around the world across communities and divides. The vast majority of people everywhere want peace, and they need our support. Sixth, we will leverage human rights as an early warning tool. We will strengthen our investigative and analytical capacities to help identify tensions before they erupt in violence. Finally, we will continue pushing for accountability, a prerequisite for sustainable peace. I urge states to strengthen domestic accountability mechanisms and to give their full backing to the International Criminal Court. I also encourage states who have yet to do so to exercise available universal jurisdiction so that those accused of atrocity crimes face justice even when domestic courts are unable or unwilling to act. Mr. President, the tragedy of conflict has touched almost all our lives. The human cost echoes down the generations, and every war has devastating impact on our health and our environment. But today, we face other threats to our rights that are unfamiliar, even unprecedented. The relationship between digital tools like AI and our human nature, our human agency, will be a priority for the years ahead. The need for AI governance is widely acknowledged, but where is the action? Delay only benefits the massive tech companies, their owners and enablers, a handful of men has almost unlimited power over AI, which we are repeatedly told has unimaginable computing capacity. They talk about freedom, but on closer inspection, this turns out to be little more than the freedom to exploit our data. There has been some recent progress at the international level. including the establishment of the global dialogue on AI and the independent international scientific panel on AI. And I welcome landmark steps on platform accountability by the European Commission and AI governance by the Republic of Korea, among others. However, I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity. AI that escapes its testing environment or blackmails developers to prevent itself from being turned off is AI that is too powerful. I'm calling here today for an all-out effort to put cast iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI before it is too late. I will be writing to AI companies in the coming days to urge them to take the steps that are within their control to reduce risks now. At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines. We need independent verification and much stronger collaboration on security within the industry. We also need to consider the human rights impacts of AI on employment practices, on fundamental principles of democracy, and on our environment. Little wonder people are rejecting AI and even refusing to use it, and governments and companies need to listen to that. Human rights offer a way to navigate these difficult issues. And I would put a particular emphasis on looking for solutions together with all those who are calling for technology that serves humanity rather than the other way around.

President, when I hear about technology leading to extraordinary progress and prosperity, I can't help asking, Where will that prosperity come from if we don't change the way we treat our planet? From scorched, exhausted, depleted land? Technology is not a magic wand. Its development needs to be matched by action on the other challenges that we face. Take the climate crisis, for instance. The massive hidden cost of fossil fuels to our health, our economies and our environment far exceeds what appears on our energy bills. The International Monetary Fund puts those costs at some $6.7 trillion a year, nearly 6% of global GDP. Heat waves in Europe have killed an estimated 35,000 people this summer. But the true toll is likely to be much higher. And none of this is inevitable. We must keep our focus on limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius as set out in the Paris Agreement by ensuring that the current overshoot is as small and as short as possible. We need to pursue investment in resilience, adaptation and early warning based on equity and solidarity. These are human rights imperatives if we are to safeguard people from disasters like the recent collapse of the glacier in Nepal and China. In Switzerland, an advanced early warning system made it possible to evacuate the entire village of Blatten before it was buried last year. Unfortunately, today's investments and innovations seem to be driven largely by profit, regardless of the costs. And these business models are squeezing our planet and its people past breaking point.

This concentration of wealth and power in one small corner of humanity is creating tensions that undermine both stability and sustainability. Yet, rather than urgently addressing these imbalances, some leaders are exploiting them. Imposing crippling tariffs on countries already under severe stress from the climate crisis, debt burdens, and inequitable tax rules weakens their political autonomy and their ability to fight poverty. With less than four years left to deliver on the 2030 agenda, only 36% of its targets are making progress, and 15% have gone into reverse. Across the world, growing numbers of people cannot afford secure housing or a healthy diet. When we celebrate economic growth, let's be honest about where this growth goes. The International Labour Organization estimates that over the past two decades it has benefited owners and investors more than workers. In several countries in sub-Saharan Africa, for example, economic growth is not matched by reductions in poverty. These injustices are putting the social contract under increasing strain. In many countries, including Albania, Argentina, India, Indonesia and Tunisia, anger over inequality, unbearable living costs, lack of basic services, unemployment and corruption has boiled over into the streets. Conversely, economies that are grounded in human rights bring stability, opportunity, and trust. They foster transparent institutions, fair taxation, and effective public spending. At a time of dwindling foreign aid, they can be instrumental in mobilizing domestic resources. Our work in Kenya illustrates this clearly. By supporting the authorities to include communities in economic decisions, we have helped address concerns that were fueling public discontent. We are working with governments in Cambodia, Iraq, Liberia, South Africa, and beyond to fight corruption, protect the rights of workers, and build economies that work for everyone. And I will continue in the coming years to push for the human rights economy to become a universal model. Human rights need to underpin all development efforts if they are to be truly sustainable. We will work to ensure that they are at the heart of global policy, including the UN Tax Convention, the International Panel on Equality, the Loss and Damage Fund, and the emerging vision for sustainable development beyond 2030. Mr. President, I will also focus on civic space and on people's right to peaceful protest, free expression, and information. These rights build trust between people and their governments. They are a bridge between frustration and dialogue, between aspirations and change. Yet, instead of engaging with the legitimate concerns of their people, many states are resorting to repression. In Iran, The authorities are using the war as a pretext to pursue even more brutal oppression. Since March 2026, 59 people have been executed on national security related charges, more than the number put to death on the same charges in the whole of 2025. Business closures linked to compulsory hijab requirements are also troubling. In Pakistan, the authorities have used excessive lethal force and arbitrary detention to quell protests. The recent protests in India showed the best response is dialogue with youth leaders, not the excessive use of force. In Nicaragua, the authorities have closed down opposition political parties. In the Russian Federation, the authorities have continued to suppress the opposition and bar parties from participating in elections. Restrictions on civic space and media freedoms are deepening from Azerbaijan, Georgia and the Russian Federation to Tunisia and Uganda. And I deplore the prohibition of demonstrations across Afghanistan by the de facto authorities. Digital surveillance is becoming an increasingly powerful tool of repression in several countries, including Angola, Myanmar and Serbia. Ahead of elections in Bosnia, I urge political leaders to counter hate speech and discrimination and to end the glorification of war criminals. In Venezuela, all arbitrarily detained people need to be released, and my team granted immediate access to all places of detention. I welcome Mexico's adoption of a protocol to investigate crimes committed against human rights defenders. Mr. President, a tide of systemic discrimination is sweeping around the world. Across regions, femicide is an alarming trend. In recent weeks, for example, seven women were reportedly killed by current or former partners in Italy, and nine women were reportedly killed in Cameroon. Huge data gaps make this crime particularly difficult to track. Legislation and prosecution are crucial, but we also need to address root causes. discrimination, inequality and gender stereotypes. Studies show higher rates of femicide and other violence against women are linked to broader social tensions and an increased likelihood of violent conflict. In Libya, I hope the new political agreement will create the momentum to adopt the law on violence against women, which has been pending for years. I again call on the de facto authorities in Afghanistan to rescind their appalling decrees and policies effectively criminalizing the presence of women and girls in public life. Their system of severe discrimination and oppression, now in its sixth year, is nothing short of gender-based apartheid. LGBTIQ+ people are facing growing threats. In Burkina Faso, Niger, and Senegal, authorities have arrested people under discriminatory laws. And Kyrgyzstan, Portugal, the United Kingdom, and the United States are adopting or considering restrictions on the equal rights of transgender people. Racism is one of society's deepest ills. Hard-won gains for people of African descent are deliberately being undermined in some countries, including cuts to anti-discrimination programs and attempts to distort history. Politicians, traditional and social media amplify isolated incidents to portray migrants, refugees, Muslims, marginalized racial and ethnic groups, and minorities as a collective threat. In some countries, such depictions have led to attacks against entire communities. I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries. Four more people have died in U.S. immigration custody since my last update to this Council, for a total of 23 deaths in 2016 alone. There needs to be accountability for these deaths. I am concerned that plans to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves will increase the violence associated with their operations. In China, tightening restrictions on the rights of the Tibetan people, including their freedom of religion, are deeply troubling, and I appeal for an urgent U-turn on these policies. But in some places where human rights are under serious strain, people are demonstrating their agency and power by marching, documenting abuses, lobbying parliamentarians, and building solidarity networks. In South Africa, civil society pressure contributed to gender-based violence and femicide being declared a national disaster in November 2025. These are acts of humanity, and I commend them. Mr. President, our action in the years ahead will be inspired by these movements, which leverage human rights to navigate between extremes. At the national and the local level, this means working closely with marginalized communities. We will stand in solidarity with them, elevate their voices, and support their efforts. The Global Alliance for Human Rights will be our entry point to increase engagement not only with states, but with civil society and others. We will also increase our outreach to excluded or marginalized groups, including indigenous peoples, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ people, religious minorities, stateless and undocumented people, the unhoused, street children, migrants and refugees. Because standing up for each other is what human rights are for. We will strengthen our work with governments on justice systems, including incarceration practices. Prisons are too often used as a dumping ground for people who don't fit in and a substitute for addressing the root causes of social problems. They may also become hotbeds of radicalization and extremism. I remain deeply concerned by the situation in China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, including in detention facilities, and I again urge the authorities to review national security and counter-terrorism legislation, strengthen the protection of minorities, and investigate allegations of human rights violations, including torture. I call on them to follow up on the recommendations made by my office and UN human rights mechanisms. I also encourage full implementation of the National Action Plan for Human Rights, which is welcome. We will strengthen our efforts around the world to end the use of the death penalty, which overwhelmingly targets minorities, people living in poverty, and dissenting voices. We will continue to call out the sharp rise in executions in a small number of states. We will build on our work with governments to address militarized approaches to security and law enforcement that are deeply counterproductive. I know many of you are uncomfortable with what is done in the name of protecting national security. These outdated practices can be an albatross around the neck of government. How do you tame the beast? Again, that's what human rights are for. In Bangladesh, we have been calling for a strengthened and independent national institution that has oversight of security forces. We will continue our work with governments around the world, including in Central Asia, to advance inclusive social and economic policies that deliver for everyone. President, at the global level,

we will be relentless in working to strengthen international law and the human rights ecosystem that benefits us all. It's clear that some powers want to destroy all efforts at multilateral cooperation and replace them with transactional deal-making. They are undermining global cooperation on climate, on health, on women's reproductive rights and beyond. If you want to know where this leads, look at the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The weakening of global health systems and reduced funding has made it worse, and it continues to pose a threat across borders. Despite all this, global accountability still exists. Ask Bosnians, ask Filipinos, ask Chileans. This is a long-term project and our work documenting abuses is essential to it.

Universality is a plank of accountability. Equal standards for all are essential. That is the basis of our tried and tested methodology to monitor and report on human rights violations and abuses and our engagement with all countries. Universality is fundamental to the treaty bodies and special procedures mandate holders. The upcoming Secretary General's report on the treaty body system will show that this crucial work is endangered by chronic underfunding and a liquidity crisis, and I call for your support. In the next four years, I intend to bring proposals for greater rationalization, innovation and creativity to the human rights ecosystem through continuous improvement, building on our own reform efforts and other initiatives as part of the UN80 process. Mr. President, power dynamics at the global and national level have changed, and we are changing in response. The Global Alliance for Human Rights, the first of its kind, will be a place where everyone working for human rights makes common cause and stands up to the anti-rights onslaught. governments, civil society, philanthropists, the corporate sector, academia, young people, artists, cities, local government, and many others will be able to co-create solutions to the human rights challenges that we face. The alliance will showcase how human rights connect people through facts, compassion, and the law. In its initial phase, the Global Alliance will aim to put human rights education into every classroom, promote digital innovation and business practices with a human face, and help cities all over the world to deliver for their residents. And this is just the beginning. I urge you to join and play a full part. What drives us is the belief that human rights will help people of all our societies to realize their hopes and aspirations in the spirit of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which affirmed that everyone everywhere is born free and equal in dignity and rights. This means holding up a mirror to those in power, challenging the status quo, and pushing the boundaries. Robust debate, critical thinking, differences and disagreements are part of the age-old struggle for human rights. The only way to advance is through honest discussion, genuine engagement, and working together. We will always talk to everyone, and we will never give up on anyone. Human rights are carriers of hope. They are a compass in turbulent times, and they offer concrete solutions to our challenges. And I look forward to continuing this important work with you. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. High Commissioner for Human Rights. We will now take a short technical break before holding the interactive dialogue with the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan. They start by seeing my face on the screen. I think everybody can start settling down. We have a very tight schedule, so I would encourage all colleagues to settle down and we shall begin with the session. Even the Indonesian delegation is not sitting down. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, Let us now begin with the interactive dialogue on the report of the Independent Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, pursuant to Council Resolution 60/13. It is also my honor to welcome the distinguished members of the fact-finding mission for the Sudan, Mr. Mohamed Chande Othman, Ms. Joy Ngozi Ezilo, and Ms. Mona Rishwani. The list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I know many of you are excited to meet friends and colleagues after the summer break and all, but we do really need a bit of silence in the room. So can I ask colleagues to, you are welcome to continue your conversation, but maybe lower your voice a bit so the substantive part of our gathering can take place and the social side can take place maybe elsewhere or with a lower volume. Thanks very much. And I now give the floor to Mr. Chande Othman for the introductory remarks. And the floor is yours, sir. Thank you.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, Our report, "Fueling Sudan's Conflict: Weapons, Fighters, and External Support Networks," highlights two key, closely connected findings. First, how weapons technology, particularly long-range drones, has redefined the battlefields. Second, how these advanced military capabilities are being sustained through external support. including weapons, technology, logistics, training, and personnel. Mr. President, both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces are increasingly using long-range drones, resulting in attacks now reaching far beyond traditional front lines and with devastating consequences for civilians. Civilians have been harmed in their homes, schools, hospitals, markets, displacement sites and places of refuge, and while also attending weddings, funerals and other community gatherings. The impact of these drones cannot be measured by counting civilian casualties alone, but must be understood through the services lost, the infrastructure destroyed, and the lasting disruption to daily life. In July, this Council requested us to urgently investigate the situation in and around El Obeid, North Kordofan, and to update you during this session. That investigation is ongoing. Repeated RSF drone attacks affected electricity, fuel, and other key infrastructure that civilians depended on for water, healthcare, and transport. These attacks underscore that risks remain acute as civilians continue to face repeated aerial threat, displacement, and pressure on already strained essential services in a city under partial siege. In Kallogi, South Kordofan, Successive RSF drone strikes on a kindergarten and a hospital harmed not only those caught in the initial attacks, but also those trying to assist the wounded. As a result, 114 were killed, including 60 children. In Dayan, East Darfur, Sudanese Armed Forces strikes rendered Al-Dayan Teaching Hospital nonfunctional, killing at least 70 people and depriving more than 2 million people of access to critical health services. In Nyabol, Blue Nile State, Sudanese Armed Forces drones attacks struck the main market and nearby water infrastructure, causing extensive damage to shops and markets. Women and children continue to bear a heavy burden. They are repeatedly among the dead and injured. The attacks often deepen existing inequalities and barriers to essential services. In Olobaid, the Benatini Hospital suspended operations after a nearby drone strike by RSF damaged operating theatres and the pharmacy. For children, the destruction of schools, health facilities, and other civilian infrastructure affects not only their safety today, but also their future development and well-being. Based on the evidence gathered, we found reasonable grounds to believe that both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces committed serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law, which may amount to war crimes. The report also examined how this conflict is being fueled through external interference and material support. We found reasonable grounds to believe The transnational network facilitated RSF military operations, linking individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, southeastern Libya, and Puntland in Somalia. Using air, land, and sea routes, the network supplied weapons, drone-related equipment, military materiel, logistical assistance, and personnel to Nyala and other RSF-held areas in Sudan. The evidence also indicates the former Colombian military personnel were recruited, trained, and deployed to support the RSF. They played an integral role in RSF drones operations, operating and maintaining drone systems, and training personnel, including before and during the takeover of El Fasher, where we had documented conduct bearing the hallmarks of genocide. Thank you. I give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of North Macedonia.

Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malta.

Thank you. I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic.

Thank you. Distinguished representative colleagues, this was the last speaker we could accommodate. President, ladies and gentlemen, members of the Human Rights Council and of the FFM, my thanks first and foremost to the FFM members for the report. Mr. President, Lawyers for Lawyers, the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute, and Lawyers Rights Watch Canada thank the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for its continued work. This year alone, at least 31 lawyers were reportedly suspended or disbarred by disciplinary bodies lacking a recognized legal mandate. These attacks severely undermine the protection and independence of lawyers, further eroding the rule of law in Sudan and leaving civilians increasingly without effective legal protection amid the ongoing conflict, particularly those facing charges carrying the death penalty. We urge this Council to respond robustly to the ever-worsening situation in Sudan by extending the mission's mandate in full for another two years and equipping it with the resources it needs to adequately investigate ongoing human rights violations, including against lawyers, in advance of accountability. We thank you.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, I thank you for the support to the work of Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan and for the solidarity for the people of Sudan that you have expressed. I think from your intervention, it's clear that protection of Sudanese civilians is imperative and accountability is a paramount consideration. even in negotiating peace. The expanding use of drones sustained by external weapons, technology, financing personnel has brought the violence into the places where ordinary life should continue. It has turned maternity wards, classrooms, water points, and shelter, including IDP camps, into sites of fear and loss. At the heart of this is not only a report about weapon flows or military capability. It is a report about people. And we should remind ourselves that this is a report about people, about mothers searching for care where hospitals are struck, children killed when they should have been learning or playing, families displaced once and then attacked again, and communities forced to survive under a sky that has become a The evidence demands more attention. It demands action from every state and actor with the power to stop the support that exacerbates this conflict. External support is not a side issue in Sudan's conflict. On the issue of question asked by Switzerland with regard to El Obeid, obviously the intervention and the discussion as an urgent discussion on this issue helped to ameliorate rate, even though the fear of and the siege is continuing. I want to say that the Council should send, I plead, Just like we've done a lot of recommendation, which is very clear from the report, an unmistakable message that civilian life in Sudan is not expendable. Thank you very much for your feedback and the very important questions that you have asked us. I will address three issues together to group some of your concerns. First, the conduct of the parties to the conflict and the role of external actors. Our findings show how weapons, financing, personnel, and technology from outside Sudan are expanding the party's military capabilities and enabling sophisticated operations with devastating consequences for the civilians, as my colleague, Joy, just mentioned. External support cannot be separated from the conduct of those receiving it. The gravity of the violations and the foreseeable risk of recurrence are documented. Those providing support must exercise due diligence, ensure that their assistance does not contribute to violations or international crimes, investigate illicit activities within their jurisdiction, and halt them. Denial is not enough. Action is needed. Actors with influence over the parties must use their diplomatic and economic leverage to secure compliance with international law and protect civilians. This is why we have called for the strict enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and its extension to the whole of Sudan. The conflict is spreading as the parties require more technologies, with long-range drones reaching Kordofan, Blue Nile, and White Nile. The second issue several of you asked about is the impact on women and children. Sexual and gender-based violence remains a defining feature of this conflict. Thirdly, and I'll switch into Arabic, we cannot protect civilians without achieving justice and accountability. These efforts have to start by protecting survivors and victims and witnesses, and to put an end to intimidation of those who cooperate with the different mechanisms, and to have evidences to be used before the court. I want to say that intimidation and reprisals are on the increase by the parties to the conflict.

The ICJ, the ICC must be supported and cooperated with. Its jurisdiction must cover all violations around the Sudan, not only in Darfur. As I mentioned, these violations, these crimes are increasing by the day. the international legal jurisdiction must also be exercised to prosecute the perpetrators wherever they are. We also call for tribunals specifically for the Sudan in cooperation with the ICC in order to realize a widespread and more effective accountability in order to increase Trust between parties. We support the trust, the confidence-building measures as proposed by the High Commissioner for Human Rights. We call upon all parties to engage constructively and to be flexible. In this respect, we also support all efforts of mediation and to establish accountability in the peace process. Our message today is clear. Thank you. This brings us to the end of this interactive dialogue. I wish to thank the members of the fact-finding mission for their participation and their contribution. We will now take a short technical break before holding the enhanced interactive dialogue on the situation of human rights of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in Myanmar. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, we will now begin the Enhanced Interactive Dialogue on the situation of human rights of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in Myanmar. It is my honor to welcome Mr. Walker Turk, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. Also allow me to welcome the distinguished panelists, Mr. Nicholas Kumjian, head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, Ms. Kaoru Okizumi, Mr. Tun Khin, Mr. Tin Zar Shun Lee Yi, and Ms. Zoya Fan. list of speakers will close after 15 minutes and I now have the honor to give the floor to the High Commissioner for Human Rights for his statement. You have the floor, sir.

Mr. President, Excellencies, colleagues, the human rights crisis in Myanmar is a matter of the greatest international concern. The report and the discussion is further evidence of this. The devastating regional impacts of the crisis are clearer by the day. Millions of people have been forced from their homes and hundreds have died on dangerous sea crossings. Illegal economic activity is flourishing with an impact on the environment and economies throughout the region. Soaring humanitarian needs and reduced funding are undermining basic services, creating a real risk that diseases like cholera could spread across borders. Credible sources have verified the killing of more than 1,200 civilians during the reporting period. Open sources indicate that the actual figure may be more than 3,000. Airstrikes remained the main cause of civilian deaths, confirming military's disregard for calls to end hostilities and protect civilians. Forced conscription has become a key tactic used by the military to sustain its advances on the battlefield, control the population and spread fear. The military's denial and instrumentalization of aid have worsened the situation, particularly in minority areas. The catastrophic situation of the Rohingya is a wound that affects the entire country and other states, particularly Bangladesh. Rohingya in Rakhine are subjected to widespread and systematic human rights violations and abuses, including arbitrary arrests, torture, sexual and gender-based violence, enforced disappearance, forced labour and recruitment by both the military and the Arakan Army. I am particularly concerned by the seizure of land by the Arakan Army in Rohingya areas. This makes their plight even worse and their return home even more challenging. Much of my professional life has been dedicated to protecting the Rohingya. Their unspeakable suffering over decades has to end, and the involvement of the international community is absolutely essential. Mr. President, Illegal businesses are taking full advantage of the collapse of the rule of law in Myanmar. Drugs, scam centers, and illegal mines are blighting lives, denying the people of Myanmar the use of their own resources, and fueling the conflict through payments to the military. Myanmar is the leading global producer of opium and methamphetamines. and scam centers have expanded along border areas and in major cities, causing major concerns around fraud, kidnapping, human trafficking, slavery, sexual violence, and exploitation. Rare earth mining sites have surged by more than 150% since the coup, causing air pollution and contaminating rivers on both sides of Myanmar's border with Thailand. The use of highly destructive mining techniques has led to rampant deforestation and runoff water saturated with radioactive elements and toxic chemicals, including arsenic and lead. This contamination poses risks to drinking water and river-based livelihoods in neighboring Thailand and the wider Mekong Basin. Mining operations also rely on exploitative labor practices and subject people, particularly women, to deadly hazards, institutionalized abuse, and systematic sexual violence. Mr. President, we are here today because efforts to resolve the crisis over many years have been insufficient. It is clear that if this continues, the situation will deteriorate further and prospects for resolution will become even more distant. Myanmar is testing the credibility of the international community's expressed desire for change, particularly since the military staged elections in an attempt to gain international recognition. Engagement is important, but it must be founded on human rights. Efforts to normalize relations without any sign whatsoever that the military are complying with fundamental obligations and international law will only fuel even greater violence and violations against civilians in Myanmar and beyond. The very grim human rights picture I have painted is a reality check on all those who could bring influence to bear who are pretending that the situation is different. The International Court of Justice's upcoming determination on the merits of the case of genocide brought by the Gambia and others will be vitally important. All countries need to use their leverage to press for change and find new ways to push for progress. We need more than so-called calibrated engagement. We need human rights-based engagement. This should be conditioned on benchmarks that demonstrate a genuine commitment by the military to ending violence, allowing humanitarian access, and releasing all those arbitrarily detained. It should prioritize accountability, including for atrocity crimes committed against the Rohingya. Engagement should not legitimize a system that has disregarded all demands for restraint and committed endless violations. I urge Member States to refer the full situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court through the Security Council and to end transfers to Myanmar of arms, ammunition, jet fuel and dual-use items where there is a clear risk they could facilitate violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. There can be no question of returning Rohingya and other refugees to Myanmar at a time of such insecurity and danger. Such returns would constitute a flagrant breach of the non-refoulement principle. And I call for all states to support the people of Myanmar politically and financially in their demands for democracy, justice, and human rights. Thank you.

Thank you, High Commissioner. We are going to use remaining time to hear all the presentations by the panel. And I now give the floor to Mr. Nicholas Kungjan, the head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar.

Mr. President, thank you. Excellencies, it is an honor to present the eighth annual report of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar. Unfortunately, I must report that the situation in Myanmar continues to deteriorate. Serious international crimes are being committed with greater frequency and intensity. The Myanmar military is increasingly relying on aerial attacks, and civilians are the principal victims. Attacks escalated in the run-up to the elections completed in January and have continued unabated. Two weeks ago, the military bombed a monastery in Sagaing region during a Buddhist retreat, one of more than 800 aerial attacks on religious buildings since the military coup. Schools and hospitals are also frequently hit. The Myanmar military is making greater use of paramotors and drones, which are harder to detect than planes, giving people less time to seek shelter. We have also observed an increase in double-tap attacks, where a second attack hits first responders and those helping the wounded. Our investigations are progressing. We have identified a number of units involved in these attacks and the air bases from which they operate. We have also advanced investigations into torture in military-run detention facilities and identified commanders and interrogators. Our evidence includes accounts of horrific sexual and gender-based crimes, including gang rape and the burning of genitals with cigarettes. Mr. President, our mandate from the Council is to investigate serious international crimes committed in Myanmar. We collect evidence of such crimes regardless of the political loyalty, ethnicity, or religion of the perpetrators or the victims. In Rakhine State, the conflict has intensified significantly, and we are investigating allegations of killings, arbitrary detention, torture, and forced displacement committed by various armed groups. All ethnicities in Rakhine State have suffered from these crimes. Many Rakhine and other groups have been victims of aerial bombings, artillery attacks, and obstructions to humanitarian assistance. Rohingya and other minorities caught between the combatants continue to take enormous risks to escape the violence Since early 2024, more than 154,000 Rohingya have crossed into Bangladesh, joining close to a million others who cannot safely return home as the violence and insecurity in Rakhine continues. We have collected substantial evidence from more than 1,600 sources, including videos, photographs, geospatial imagery, social media posts, and information on bank transactions and weapons supply chains. We have collected over 750 testimonies from witnesses. This evidence is helping us establish what crimes happened, who was responsible, and who may have financed, facilitated, or benefited from these crimes. The Mechanism has shared extensive evidence and analysis with authorities pursuing accountability for crimes committed against the Rohingya, including at the International Criminal Court and in the Argentine District Court. We have also shared information concerning crimes committed since the 2021 military takeover with authorities from several States.
